pos: n. (a short two-edged blade; rendering Hebrew chereb)
etymology: From Old French dague. A dagger is a short blade, concealable — which is exactly why Ehud made one.
biblical_def: A dagger is a short blade. Ehud makes his to a specification: “a dagger which had two edges, of a cubit length; and he did gird it under his raiment upon his right thigh” (Jdg 3:16). Because he was left-handed the weapon sat where no guard would search, and he told Eglon, “I have a message from God unto thee” before drawing it (Jdg 3:20–21). Hebrews later describes a different two-edged blade: the word of God, sharper than any twoedged sword (Heb 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dagger as a short sword; a poniard; and a small weapon, which may be concealed under the clothes.
webster_full: DAGGER, n. A short sword; a poniard.
2. In fencing schools, a blunt blade of iron with a basket hilt, used for defense.
3. With printers, an obelisk, or obelus, a mark of reference in the form of a dagger.
scriptures: Jdg 3:16
But Ehud made him a dagger which had two edges, of a cubit length; and he did gird it under his raiment upon his right thigh.
Jdg 3:20
And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat. a
Jdg 3:21
And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly:
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Deliverers are expected to arrive with obvious credentials, and Judges keeps sending men with a disability, a wrong-handed weapon, or no army at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 3:15 introduces Ehud with a detail the narrative then makes decisive: a man lefthanded. The Hebrew is literally bound of his right hand — possibly an impairment. He forged a two-edged blade of a cubit and strapped it to his right thigh, where a guard checking a right-handed man's left side would never look. What made him unsuitable by the world's reckoning is precisely what got him past the door.

The pattern runs through Judges. A left-handed man, a woman with a tent peg, a farmer threshing in a winepress, a man with three hundred torches. Paul's summary of God's method — God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty — is not a New Testament innovation. It is a description of how the book of Judges works.
roots_summary: Hebrew chereb (H2719), a sword or cutting instrument; pi-photh, two mouths — the Hebrew idiom for double-edged.
roots_lines: Hebrew chereb (H2719) — sword, dagger; Judges 3:16, 21-22.
Hebrew gomed (H1574) — a cubit, short measure; only Judges 3:16, the blade's length.
Greek distomos (G1366) — two-edged, two-mouthed; Hebrews 4:12, Revelation 1:16.
usage: “A dagger which had two edges… upon his right thigh” — hidden where no guard would search.
“I have a message from God unto thee” — spoken before the blade was drawn.
“Sharper than any twoedged sword” — the word that divides deeper.

etymology: From Old French daintie, worth or value. Dainties are choice foods, and Scripture is consistently suspicious of them at another man's table.
biblical_def: Dainties are delicacies. Proverbs warns twice: “be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat” (Pro 23:3), and “eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats” (Pro 23:6). Jacob prepares savoury meat for Isaac (Gen 27:9 in the same idiom), and Revelation lists among Babylon's losses “all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee” (Rev 18:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dainty as something nice, tender and delicate to the taste; a delicacy; and as an adjective, nice, delicate, affectedly fine.
webster_full: DAINTY, a. Nice; pleasing to the palate; of exquisite taste; delicious; as dainty food.
2. Delicate; of acute sensibility; nice in selecting what is tender and good; squeamish; soft; effeminate.
DAINTY, n. Something nice and delicate to the taste; that which is exquisitely delicious; a delicacy.
scriptures: Pro 23:3
Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat.
Pro 23:6
Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats:
And the fruits that thy soul lusted after are departed from thee, and all things which were dainty and goodly are departed from thee, and thou shalt find them no more at all.
Pro 23:1
When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee:
corruption_summary: Hospitality from the powerful is accepted as friendship, and Proverbs calls a rich man's delicacies deceitful meat — food that is a transaction.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 23:1-3 gives the setting and the reason: when thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee… be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat. The food is called deceitful not because it is poisoned but because it is not what it appears to be. It looks like generosity and functions as an investment. A man enjoying the table is being placed under obligation while his guard is down and his appetite is up.

Verse 6 sharpens it further: eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye… for as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee. The host's words and his heart run in opposite directions, and the guest discovers it later. Proverbs ends the passage bluntly — the morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words.
roots_summary: Hebrew matammim (H4303), savoury food, dainties; manaam (H4574), delicacies; lechem kezabim, bread of lies — deceitful meat.
roots_lines: Hebrew matammim (H4303) — dainties, savoury meat; Proverbs 23:3, 6, Genesis 27:4-31.
Hebrew manaam (H4574) — dainties; only Psalm 141:4, let me not eat of their dainties.
Greek liparos (G3045) — dainty, sumptuous; only Revelation 18:14.
usage: “Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are deceitful meat” — food that is a transaction.
“Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee” — words and heart opposed.
“All things which were dainty and goodly are departed” — Babylon's inventory, gone.

pos: n. (the quality of misleading; rendering Greek apate)
etymology: From deceit, Latin decipere, to ensnare. Deceitfulness is not a lie told but a capacity to mislead built into a thing.
biblical_def: Deceitfulness is the power to mislead. Christ names it as a thorn: the seed among thorns is he that heareth the word, “and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful” (Mat 13:22). Hebrews warns the church against being “hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb 3:13). Jeremiah says the heart is “deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deceitfulness as tendency to mislead or deceive; and the disposition to deceive.
webster_full: DECEITFULNESS, n. Tendency to mislead or deceive.
2. The disposition to deceive.
DECEITFUL, a. Tending to mislead, deceive or ensnare; as deceitful words.
scriptures: He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful.
Heb 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Heb 3:12
Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God.
corruption_summary: Deception is expected to come from outside, and Scripture locates the most effective source in the hearer's own heart and his own money.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 3:13 prescribes an unusual remedy: exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. The hardening is gradual and the deceit is what makes it invisible — nobody notices the day their conscience got quieter. Notice the remedy is not private vigilance but daily mutual exhortation. Scripture assumes a man cannot detect his own hardening and assigns the task to his brothers.

Matthew 13:22 names riches as a specific carrier: the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word. Wealth deceives not by promising to make a man wicked but by quietly persuading him he is secure. The seed in that soil is not killed by opposition; it is crowded. Nothing dramatic happens — he becometh unfruitful, and that is the whole verdict.
roots_summary: Greek apate (G539), deceit, delusion; apatao (G538), to deceive; Hebrew aqob (H6121), crooked, deceitful — of the heart in Jeremiah 17:9.
roots_lines: Greek apate (G539) — deceitfulness; Matthew 13:22, Hebrews 3:13, Ephesians 4:22.
Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; Jeremiah 17:9 — the root also behind Jacob's name.
Greek skleruno (G4645) — to harden; Hebrews 3:13, lest any of you be hardened.
usage: “The deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” — crowded rather than killed.
“Lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” — and the remedy is one another.
“The heart is deceitful above all things” — the nearest deceiver.

pos: n. (one who rescues; rendering Hebrew palat, Greek rhuomai)
etymology: From deliver, Latin deliberare, to set free. A deliverer is one who gets someone out — and Scripture assigns the title to God and to men He raises up.
biblical_def: A deliverer rescues. David piles the titles up: “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2). Judges records that God “raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel” (Jdg 3:9). Stephen says of Moses that God sent him “to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush” (Act 7:35), and Paul quotes Isaiah: “there shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Rom 11:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deliverer as one who delivers or rescues; a preserver; and one who relates or communicates.
webster_full: DELIVERER, n. One who delivers; one who releases or rescues; a preserver.
2. One who relates, or communicates.
scriptures: Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Jdg 3:9
And when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
Act 7:35
This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.
And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob:
corruption_summary: Deliverance is expected through the channels a people already trust, and Stephen's sermon turns on Israel rejecting the deliverer God actually sent.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 7:35 is the hinge of Stephen's sermon and it cost him his life: this Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer. He is drawing a pattern — the deliverer is refused first and vindicated afterward — and his hearers understood exactly where the pattern was heading before he finished.

Judges 3:9 states the cycle's mechanism in one verse: when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer. The crying comes first and the deliverer is raised, not found. Israel never once produced its own rescuer; the book records seven cycles and in each the initiative is God's. That is why Psalm 18 stacks the titles — rock, fortress, deliverer — onto one Person rather than distributing them.
roots_summary: Hebrew palat (H6403), to escape, deliver; moshia (H3467), saviour, deliverer; Greek rhuomai (G4506), to draw out of danger.
roots_lines: Hebrew palat (H6403) — to deliver, rescue; Psalm 18:2, 48, 40:17.
Hebrew moshia (H3467) — saviour, deliverer; Judges 3:9, 15, Obadiah 21.
Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to rescue, deliver; Romans 11:26, 2 Corinthians 1:10, Matthew 6:13.
usage: “My rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” — titles stacked on one Person.
“The LORD raised up a deliverer” — raised, not found.
“This Moses whom they refused… the same did God send” — the pattern that cost Stephen his life.

etymology: From Latin destituere, to forsake or set down. To be destitute is to have been left without — the word carries abandonment as well as want.
biblical_def: Destitute means wholly lacking. The psalmist prays, “he will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer” (Psa 102:17). Hebrews describes the faithful who wandered “being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (of whom the world was not worthy)” (Heb 11:37–38). James asks what profit there is in telling a brother “destitute of daily food” to be warmed and filled (Jas 2:15–16), and Paul warns of men “destitute of the truth” (1Ti 6:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines destitute as wanting; not having; deprived; and needy; abject; comfortless; friendless.
webster_full: DESTITUTE, a. Wanting; not having; deprived of; without.
2. Needy; abject; comfortless; friendless.
DESTITUTE, v.t. To forsake; to leave destitute.
scriptures: He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Jas 2:15
If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food,
Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.
corruption_summary: Words of comfort are treated as help, and James asks what profit there is in wishing a hungry man warm without giving him anything.
corruption_paragraphs: James 2:15-16 is uncomfortably concrete: if a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit? The words are kind, sincere, and worthless. James is not attacking sympathy; he is denying that sympathy expressed without provision counts as anything at all.

Hebrews 11:37-38 places destitution in an unexpected column: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (of whom the world was not worthy). The parenthesis reverses every appearance. The world looked at them and saw failures; the writer says the world was not good enough for them. Destitution in that chapter is not evidence of God's absence but a category of faith's outcome alongside the ones who stopped the mouths of lions.
roots_summary: Greek hustereo (G5302), to lack, come short; leipo (G3007), to be wanting; Hebrew arar (H6199), destitute, stripped.
roots_lines: Hebrew arar (H6199) — destitute, naked; only Psalm 102:17.
Greek hustereo (G5302) — to be destitute, lack; Hebrews 11:37, Luke 15:14.
Greek leipo (G3007) — to be wanting; James 2:15, destitute of daily food.
usage: “He will regard the prayer of the destitute” — the prayer specifically not despised.
“Being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (of whom the world was not worthy)” — the appearance reversed.
“Be ye warmed and filled… what doth it profit?” — kind words priced at nothing.

pos: v. (to put off; rendering Hebrew achar and arak)
etymology: From Latin differre, to postpone. Deferral in Scripture is examined from both sides — the pain of waiting and the wisdom of delay.
biblical_def: To defer is to put off. Proverbs names the cost: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life” (Pro 13:12). It also commends restraint: “The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression” (Pro 19:11). Ecclesiastes warns, “defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” concerning a vow (Ecc 5:4), and Daniel prays, “O Lord, hear… defer not, for thine own sake” (Dan 9:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines defer as to delay; to put off; to postpone to a future time; and to refer, to leave to another's judgment and determination.
webster_full: DEFER, v.t. To delay; to put off; to postpone to a future time; as, to defer the execution of a design.
2. To refer; to leave to another's judgment and determination.
DEFER, v.i. To yield to another's opinion; to submit to.
scriptures: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Dan 9:19
O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for thine own sake, O my God: for thy city and thy people are called by thy name.
corruption_summary: Delay is read as denial, and Proverbs grants the sickness of deferred hope without concluding the hope was misplaced.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 13:12 is unusually gentle toward the waiting: hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life. The sickness is granted as real rather than rebuked as unbelief. And the second clause does not promise everything arrives, only that arrival, when it comes, is life-giving out of proportion to the wait. Scripture's honesty about the interval is part of why its promises can be believed.

Proverbs 19:11 uses the same verb approvingly in a different direction: the discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression. Anger deferred is not anger denied; it is anger held long enough for judgment to catch up with it. And the second clause raises the standard — not merely to delay the response but to decline it, which is called a man's glory.
roots_summary: Hebrew achar (H309), to delay, defer; arak (H748), to be long, prolong — deferreth his anger is literally makes his anger long; mashak (H4900), to draw out.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashak (H4900) — to draw out, defer; Proverbs 13:12, hope deferred.
Hebrew arak (H748) — to prolong, defer; Proverbs 19:11, deferreth his anger.
Hebrew achar (H309) — to delay, tarry; Ecclesiastes 5:4, Daniel 9:19.
usage: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick” — the sickness granted as real.
“The discretion of a man deferreth his anger” — held long enough for judgment.
“Defer not, for thine own sake” — Daniel's ground for urgency.

etymology: Old English deorc. Scripture uses darkness for ignorance, for judgment, and once for the place where God chose to dwell.
biblical_def: Dark means without light. The psalmist says God “made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies” (Psa 18:11). Solomon says at the dedication, “The LORD said that he would dwell in the thick darkness” (1Ki 8:12). Paul says we see now “through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1Co 13:12), and Peter calls prophecy “a light that shineth in a dark place” until the day dawn (2Pe 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dark as destitute of light; obscure; and gloomy; disheartening; having unfavorable prospects; also, obscure, not easily understood or explained.
webster_full: DARK, a. Destitute of light; obscure. A dark atmosphere is one which prevents vision.
2. Wholly or partially black; having the quality opposite to white.
3. Gloomy; disheartening; having unfavorable prospects.
4. Obscure; not easily understood or explained.
5. Mysterious; as, the ways of Providence are often dark to human reason.
scriptures: Then spake Solomon, The LORD said that he would dwell in the thick darkness.
He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Darkness is treated as God's absence, and Solomon dedicated the temple by saying the LORD had said He would dwell in thick darkness.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 8:12 is spoken at the highest moment of Israel's history, with the cloud filling the house so the priests could not stand to minister. Solomon's first words are: the LORD said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. The glory was so present that it produced obscurity. That single sentence guards against equating darkness with divine absence, and it explains why the holiest room in the building had no window.

1 Corinthians 13:12 gives the honest present condition: for now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. Paul places himself inside the limitation rather than above it. The chapter on love ends by admitting how little the apostle who wrote it could see, which is a useful check on anyone certain they have the whole picture.
roots_summary: Hebrew choshek (H2822), darkness; araphel (H6205), thick darkness — the cloud of Sinai and the temple; Greek skotos (G4655), darkness.
roots_lines: Hebrew araphel (H6205) — thick darkness, gloom; 1 Kings 8:12, Exodus 20:21, Psalm 97:2.
Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; Genesis 1:2, Psalm 18:11.
Greek ainigma (G135) — an enigma; 1 Corinthians 13:12, darkly, literally in a riddle.
usage: “He would dwell in the thick darkness” — glory producing obscurity.
“Now we see through a glass, darkly” — the apostle inside the limitation.
“A light that shineth in a dark place” — prophecy until the day dawn.

etymology: From death. Deadly names what kills rather than what merely harms, and James applies it to the tongue.
biblical_def: Deadly means causing death. James says of the tongue, “it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas 3:8). Mark's ending promises that if believers “drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them” (Mar 16:18). The psalmist speaks of “my deadly enemies, who compass me about” (Psa 17:9), and Ezekiel says the LORD's arrows are sent “for their destruction” (Eze 5:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deadly as that may occasion death; mortal; fatal; destructive; and implacable, aiming to kill or destroy.
webster_full: DEADLY, a. That may occasion death; mortal; fatal; destructive; as a deadly blow or wound.
2. Mortal; implacable; aiming to kill or destroy; as a deadly enemy; deadly malice.
DEADLY, adv. In a manner resembling death.
2. Mortally.
scriptures: Jas 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
Psa 17:9
From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.
They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.
Jas 3:6
And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.
corruption_summary: Speech is judged by whether it was accurate, and James classifies the tongue with poison — a thing measured by what it does in a body, not by its truth content.
corruption_paragraphs: James 3:8 uses a medical category rather than a moral one: the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. Poison is not evaluated by whether the statements are true. It is evaluated by dose and effect. Words that are entirely accurate can still function as poison in a congregation, which is exactly why James spends a chapter on the tongue without once discussing lying.

The chapter's earlier image is a fire: behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth. Both metaphors share a feature — a small quantity produces damage out of all proportion to its size, and the damage continues after the speaker has moved on. That is why James says if any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, able also to bridle the whole body.
roots_summary: Greek thanatephoros (G2287), death-bringing — only James 3:8; thanasimos (G2286), deadly, in Mark 16:18; Hebrew nephesh in the idiom deadly enemies.
roots_lines: Greek thanatephoros (G2287) — deadly, death-bearing; only James 3:8.
Greek thanasimos (G2286) — deadly; only Mark 16:18.
Greek ios (G2447) — poison, rust; James 3:8, full of deadly poison.
usage: “An unruly evil, full of deadly poison” — a medical category, not a moral one.
“How great a matter a little fire kindleth” — damage out of proportion to size.
“My deadly enemies, who compass me about” — the psalmist surrounded.

etymology: From Old French debatre, to fight down. In the KJV debate is not reasoned discussion but quarrelling — and Paul lists it among the works of a depraved mind.
biblical_def: Debate in Scripture means strife. Paul lists it in the catalogue of Romans 1: “full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity” (Rom 1:29). He fears finding it at Corinth: “lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes… and tumults” (2Co 12:20). Isaiah says God stays the rough wind “in the day of the east wind” and debates in measure (Isa 27:8), and Proverbs counsels, “debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another” (Pro 25:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines debate as contention in words or arguments; discussion for elucidating truth; strife; contention; and to contend for in words or arguments.
webster_full: DEBATE, n. Contention in words or arguments; discussion for elucidating truth; strife in argument or reasoning, between persons of different opinions.
2. Strife; contention.
3. Subject of discussion.
scriptures: Rom 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,

For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:
Pro 25:9
Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another:
Isa 27:8
In measure, when it shooteth forth, thou wilt debate with it: he stayeth his rough wind in the day of the east wind.
corruption_summary: Argument is treated as the natural mode of Christian discourse, and Paul lists debate between murder and deceit.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:29 places debate in company that should give any argumentative Christian pause: being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity. Paul is not condemning careful reasoning — his own letters are sustained argument. The word here names the appetite for contention itself, and he files it among the symptoms of a mind God has given over.

Proverbs 25:9 supplies the constructive alternative: debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another. Take the dispute to the person, not to an audience. The verse anticipates Christ's instruction in Matthew 18 by centuries, and the reason attached is reputational — lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away.
roots_summary: Greek eris (G2054), strife, contention; Hebrew rib (H7378), to contend, plead a cause — the neutral legal sense in Proverbs 25:9.
roots_lines: Greek eris (G2054) — strife, debate; Romans 1:29, 2 Corinthians 12:20, 1 Corinthians 1:11.
Hebrew rib (H7378) — to contend, plead; Proverbs 25:9, debate thy cause with thy neighbour.
Hebrew sud (H5475) — secret, counsel; the thing not to be discovered to another.
usage: “Full of envy, murder, debate, deceit” — the company it keeps.
“Lest there be debates, envyings, wraths” — Paul's fear for a church.
“Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself” — the person, not an audience.

etymology: From Latin detestari, to curse while calling the gods to witness. Detestable is the strongest available word for what God abhors.
biblical_def: Detestable means utterly abhorrent, and in the prophets it is a technical word for idols. Jeremiah charges Israel: “they set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name, to defile it” (Jer 32:34), and Ezekiel repeatedly names “all the detestable things thereof and all the abominations thereof” (Eze 5:11; 7:20; 11:18,21). The word marks the objects that made the temple unfit for the God whose name it bore.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines detestable as extremely hateful; abominable; very odious; deserving abhorrence.
webster_full: DETESTABLE, a. Extremely hateful; abominable; very odious; deserving abhorrence.
DETEST, v.t. To abhor; to abominate; to hate extremely; as, to detest crimes or meanness.
scriptures: Eze 5:11

Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity.
And they shall come thither, and they shall take away all the detestable things thereof and all the abominations thereof from thence.
Eze 7:20
As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty: but they made the images of their abominations and of their detestable things therein: therefore have I set it far from them.
But they set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name, to defile it.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as worshipping statues elsewhere, and Ezekiel's detestable things were installed inside the temple by people who still used God's name.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 5:11 states the offence and the consequence in one sentence: because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee. The detestable things were not in a rival temple; they were in His. Ezekiel 8 takes the prophet on a tour of them — an image of jealousy at the gate, creeping things portrayed on the walls, women weeping for Tammuz, and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple worshipping the sun.

Ezekiel 11:18 contains the promise that answers it, and the order matters: and they shall come thither, and they shall take away all the detestable things thereof and all the abominations thereof from thence. And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. The removal and the new heart belong to the same act of God, which is why reform that only removes objects has never yet held.
roots_summary: Hebrew shiqquts (H8251), a detestable thing, idol; toebah (H8441), abomination; gillulim (H1544), dung-idols.
roots_lines: Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — detestable thing, idol; Ezekiel 5:11, 7:20, 11:18, 21, Jeremiah 16:18.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; the constant companion word.
Hebrew gillulim (H1544) — idols; Ezekiel's contemptuous term throughout.
usage: “Thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things” — installed in His own house.
“They shall take away all the detestable things… and I will give them one heart” — removal and renewal together.
“They set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name” — the name still in use.

etymology: From Latin devovere, to vow away. In Leviticus a devoted thing is placed permanently beyond recovery — the strongest form of dedication in the law.
biblical_def: To be devoted is to be given over irrevocably. Leviticus is explicit: “No devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the LORD of all that he hath… shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD” (Lev 27:28). The psalmist prays, “stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear” (Psa 119:38). Jericho was devoted, which is why Achan's theft was fatal (Jos 6:17–18 in the same vocabulary).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devote as to appropriate by vow; to set apart or dedicate by a solemn act; to consecrate; and to give up wholly; to addict, to direct the attention wholly or chiefly.
webster_full: DEVOTE, v.t. To appropriate by vow; to set apart or dedicate by a solemn act; to consecrate.
2. To give up wholly; to addict; to direct the attention wholly or chiefly.
3. To give up; to resign.
4. To doom; to consign over.
scriptures: Notwithstanding no devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the LORD of all that he hath, both of man and beast, and of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD.
Stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear.
Jos 6:17

And the city shall be accursed, even it, and all that are therein, to the LORD: only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.
None devoted, which shall be devoted of men, shall be redeemed; but shall surely be put to death.
corruption_summary: Dedication is treated as renewable enthusiasm, and the law's devoted thing could not be sold, redeemed, or reconsidered.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 27:28 sets devotion apart from every other kind of giving: no devoted thing… shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD. Ordinary vows in that chapter could be redeemed by adding a fifth part; a devoted thing could not. It had crossed a line and could not be brought back, which is what made Achan's wedge of gold from devoted Jericho not merely theft but sacrilege.

Psalm 119:38 asks God to establish His word to a servant already described as devoted to thy fear. The devotion comes first and the request follows; the psalmist is not offering dedication in exchange for a promise but asking God to make good on a word to someone already given over. That order — given first, then asking — is the shape of most petitions in the psalm.
roots_summary: Hebrew charam (H2763), to devote, ban, utterly destroy; cherem (H2764), a devoted thing — the word behind Jericho's ban.
roots_lines: Hebrew charam (H2763) — to devote irrevocably; Leviticus 27:28-29, Joshua 6:18.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — devoted thing, ban; Joshua 7:1, 11-13 of Achan's sin.
Hebrew qodesh qodashim — most holy; Leviticus 27:28, the status conferred.
usage: “Every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD” — beyond sale or redemption.
“Who is devoted to thy fear” — the servant described before the request.
“Keep yourselves from the accursed thing” — the warning Achan ignored.

pos: n. (a going down; also lineage; rendering Greek katabasis and genealogeo)
etymology: From Latin descendere, to climb down. The KJV uses it both for a slope and for ancestry, and Hebrews exploits the second sense.
biblical_def: A descent is a going down, or a lineage. Luke places the triumphal entry “at the descent of the mount of Olives”, where the whole multitude began to rejoice and praise God (Luk 19:37). Hebrews uses the genealogical sense of Melchisedec, who is “without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life” (Heb 7:3), and says he “whose descent is not counted from them received tithes of Abraham” (Heb 7:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines descent as the act of descending; a passing from a higher to a lower place; progress downward; and extraction, lineage, birth, quality.
webster_full: DESCENT, n. Progress downward; as the descent from a higher to a lower degree.
2. Inclination downward; obliquity; declivity; slope.
3. Extraction; lineage; birth; quality.
4. A proceeding from an original or progenitor.
scriptures: And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen;
Heb 7:3
Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually.
Heb 7:6
But he whose descent is not counted from them received tithes of Abraham, and blessed him that had the promises.
Heb 7:14
For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood.
corruption_summary: Standing is inherited, and Hebrews argues Christ's priesthood precisely from the fact that His descent qualified Him for nothing under the law.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 7:14 concedes a difficulty rather than hiding it: for it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood. By the law's own genealogical rules Christ could not be a priest. The writer's answer is not to dispute the lineage but to establish a prior and higher order — Melchisedec, without descent, who blessed Abraham and received tithes from him before Levi existed.

That argument reframes what qualification means. Melchisedec is described as without father, without mother, without descent — the record supplies no genealogy, and Hebrews treats the silence as deliberate. A priesthood that rests on an endless life rather than on a family tree cannot be inherited, interrupted, or lost, which is the whole point of the chapter.
roots_summary: Greek katabasis (G2600), a descent, going down; agenealogetos (G35), without recorded genealogy — only Hebrews 7:3.
roots_lines: Greek katabasis (G2600) — descent, slope; only Luke 19:37.
Greek agenealogetos (G35) — without descent, ungenealogized; only Hebrews 7:3.
Greek genealogeo (G1075) — to trace descent; only Hebrews 7:6.
usage: “At the descent of the mount of Olives” — where the praising began.
“Without father, without mother, without descent” — a priesthood no tree supports.
“Our Lord sprang out of Juda” — the difficulty conceded, then answered.

etymology: From desire, Latin desiderare. The Hebrew root is the same as the tenth commandment's covet — desirability is measured by what draws the eye.
biblical_def: Desirable means worth desiring. Ezekiel uses it of the Assyrians Israel courted: “all of them desirable young men, captains and rulers… horsemen riding upon horses” (Eze 23:6,12,23) — a nation seduced by an impressive appearance. The same root gives the tree that was “to be desired to make one wise” (Gen 3:6) and the Messiah as “the desire of all nations” (Hag 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines desirable as worthy of desire; that is to be wished for with sincerity or earnestness; pleasing; agreeable.
webster_full: DESIRABLE, a. Worthy of desire; that is to be wished for with sincerity or earnestness.
2. Pleasing; agreeable.
scriptures: Eze 23:6
Which were clothed with blue, captains and rulers, all of them desirable young men, horsemen riding upon horses.
She doted upon the Assyrians her neighbours, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men.
Gen 3:6

And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.
Hag 2:7
And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Attraction is trusted as a guide, and Ezekiel's word for the officers who ruined Israel is the same word Eve used of the tree.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 23 is deliberately uncomfortable, and the repeated adjective is the point: all of them desirable young men, captains and rulers, clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses. Israel's foreign alliances are described as attraction to an impressive appearance. The prophet does not say the Assyrians were unattractive; he says the attraction was the mechanism of the ruin.

Genesis 3:6 uses the same root three times over: the tree was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise. Every one of those assessments was accurate. The fruit was good, it was pleasant, and it did convey a kind of knowledge. Desirability was never the disputed question; permission was, and desirability is not evidence about permission.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamad (H2530), to desire, covet — the verb of the tenth commandment; chemed (H2531), desirable; chemdah (H2532), desire, the desire of all nations.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, covet; Genesis 3:6, Exodus 20:17.
Hebrew chemed (H2531) — desirable; Ezekiel 23:6, 12, 23.
Hebrew chemdah (H2532) — desire, precious thing; Haggai 2:7, the desire of all nations.
usage: “All of them desirable young men” — the attraction as the mechanism.
“A tree to be desired to make one wise” — the assessment was accurate.
“The desire of all nations shall come” — the one desirability that is safe.

etymology: From Latin declarare, to make clear. A declaration is a matter set out plainly rather than implied.
biblical_def: A declaration is a plain public statement. Luke opens his Gospel with the word: “Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us” (Luk 1:1). Job says, “Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears” (Job 13:17), and Esther's honours are set out in the same terms (Est 10:2 in context of the declaration of Mordecai's greatness).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines declaration as an affirmation; a publication or explanation; and in law, that part of the process or pleadings in which the plaintiff sets forth at large his cause of complaint.
webster_full: DECLARATION, n. An affirmation; a publication or explanation; that which is declared or told.
2. Expression of facts, opinions, promises, predictions, etc.
3. In law, that part of the process or pleadings in which the plaintiff sets forth at large his cause of complaint.
scriptures: Luk 1:1
Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us,
Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears.
Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
corruption_summary: The Gospels are read as devotional writing, and Luke opens his by describing a research method and naming his purpose as certainty.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 1:1-4 is the most methodologically explicit preface in Scripture: it seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, that thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed. Eyewitnesses, orderly arrangement, a named recipient, and a stated aim. The word certainty is the goal, which is a strange thing to claim if the material were legend.

Job 13:17 uses the word in its legal sense, and Job's whole speech there is a court filing: hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears. Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified. A man convinced he has a case, asking to be heard rather than comforted. Scripture makes room for that posture even when the man is partly wrong.
roots_summary: Greek diegesis (G1335), a narrative, declaration — only Luke 1:1; asphaleia (G803), certainty, safety; Hebrew achavah (H262), declaration.
roots_lines: Greek diegesis (G1335) — declaration, narrative; only Luke 1:1.
Greek asphaleia (G803) — certainty; Luke 1:4, that thou mightest know the certainty.
Greek autoptes (G845) — eyewitness; Luke 1:2, the sources named.
usage: “A declaration of those things which are most surely believed” — Luke's stated project.
“That thou mightest know the certainty” — the aim named outright.
“Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration” — Job filing a case.

etymology: From Latin defendere, to ward off. Scripture's defending is chiefly God's own action, and its object is chiefly the powerless.
biblical_def: To defend is to protect. God promises Jerusalem, “As birds flying, so will the LORD of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it” (Isa 31:5). The psalmist commands the judges, “Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy” (Psa 82:3). David sings, “let them also that love thy name be joyful in thee. For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield” (Psa 5:11–12), and God says of Jerusalem, “I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake” (2Ki 19:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines defend as to drive from; to thrust back; hence, to deny, to repel a demand, charge, or accusation; to oppose; to resist; and to protect, to secure against attacks or evil.
webster_full: DEFEND, v.t. To drive from; to thrust back; hence, to deny; to repel a demand, charge, or accusation.
2. To protect; to secure against attacks or evil; to fortify against danger or violence.
3. To vindicate; to assert; to uphold; to maintain uninjured, by force or by argument.
scriptures: Isa 31:5
As birds flying, so will the LORD of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it; and passing over he will preserve it.
Psa 82:3
Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake.
Psa 5:11
But let all those that put their trust in thee rejoice: let them ever shout for joy, because thou defendest them: let them also that love thy name be joyful in thee.
corruption_summary: Institutions defend themselves first, and Psalm 82 addresses judges who had defended everyone except the poor and fatherless.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 82 is God standing in the congregation of the mighty and judging the judges: how long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked. Four imperatives, all directed at the same class of people, and the psalm ends by reminding the judges that they too shall die like men.

Isaiah 31:5 supplies one of Scripture's tenderest military images: as birds flying, so will the LORD of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it; and passing over he will preserve it. The picture is a bird hovering over a nest, and the verb passing over is the Passover word. Defence here is not a wall but a body interposed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ganan (H1598), to cover, defend; shaphat (H8199), to judge, vindicate; pasach (H6452), to pass over — the Passover verb in Isaiah 31:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew ganan (H1598) — to defend, cover; Isaiah 31:5, 37:35, 2 Kings 19:34.
Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, defend; Psalm 82:3, defend the poor and fatherless.
Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to pass over, spare; Isaiah 31:5, passing over he will preserve it.
usage: “As birds flying, so will the LORD of hosts defend Jerusalem” — a body interposed, not a wall.
“Defend the poor and fatherless” — four imperatives to judges.
“I will defend this city… for mine own sake” — the stated motive.

etymology: From deep. Scripture's depths are the sea, the grave, and the counsels of God — and the same word serves all three.
biblical_def: Depth is deepness. Micah promises, “thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic 7:19). Paul cries, “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33). He prays that believers may comprehend “the breadth, and length, and depth, and height” of Christ's love (Eph 3:18), and says nothing in all creation, height nor depth, shall separate us (Rom 8:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines depth as deepness; the distance or measure of a thing from the surface to the bottom; profoundness; extent of penetration, or of the capacity of penetrating.
webster_full: DEPTH, n. Deepness; the distance or measure of a thing from the surface to the bottom.
2. A deep place.
3. The abyss; a gulf of infinite profundity.
4. The middle or highest degree, as of winter or night.
5. Abstruseness; obscurity; that which is not easily explored.
scriptures: Mic 7:19
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Eph 3:18
May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;
Rom 8:39
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is imagined as a record kept somewhere retrievable, and Micah puts the sins in the depths of the sea.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 7:19 is deliberate about location: he will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. Not the shallows, not the shore — the depths, where nothing is recovered. The verse before asks who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and the answer offered is this disposal. Corrie ten Boom's addition, that God posts a sign saying no fishing, is not in the text but is faithful to it.

Romans 11:33 uses the same word for something unreachable in the opposite direction: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! Paul has just finished eleven chapters of the densest reasoning in Scripture, and he ends not with a summary but with a doxology about how much he cannot see.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsulah (H4688), the deep, depths; tehom (H8415), the abyss; Greek bathos (G899), depth.
roots_lines: Hebrew metsulah (H4688) — depths, deep places; Micah 7:19, Jonah 2:3.
Greek bathos (G899) — depth; Romans 11:33, Ephesians 3:18, Romans 8:39.
Greek anexereunetos (G419) — unsearchable; only Romans 11:33.
usage: “Cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” — where nothing is recovered.
“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” — eleven chapters ending in doxology.
“Nor height, nor depth… shall be able to separate us” — both directions covered.

pos: v. (to eat the chief meal; rendering Greek aristao)
etymology: From Old French disner, originally to break fast. In the Gospels dining is repeatedly the setting for confrontation and for restoration.
biblical_def: To dine is to eat a meal. A Pharisee marvels that Christ “had not first washed before dinner”, and the rebuke that follows fills a chapter (Luk 11:37–38). Joseph orders his steward to bring his brothers home, “for these men shall dine with me at noon” (Gen 43:16). And the risen Christ, having made a fire of coals on the shore, says to the disciples, “Come and dine” (Joh 21:12), before restoring Peter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dine as to eat the chief meal of the day; and to give a dinner to, to furnish with the principal meal.
webster_full: DINE, v.i. To eat the chief meal of the day. This meal seems originally to have been taken about the middle of the day.
DINE, v.t. To give a dinner to; to furnish with the principal meal; to feed.
scriptures: Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord.
And as he spake, a certain Pharisee besought him to dine with him: and he went in, and sat down to meat.
And when Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the ruler of his house, Bring these men home, and slay, and make ready; for these men shall dine with me at noon.
So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.
corruption_summary: Restoration is imagined as a formal proceeding, and Christ restored Peter over breakfast on a beach after cooking it Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: John 21 is arranged with great care. Peter had denied Christ three times beside a fire of coals in the high priest's courtyard; the risen Christ makes a fire of coals on the shore, cooks fish, says come and dine, and then asks three questions. The setting is not incidental. The same smell, the same number, and a meal instead of an interrogation.

Christ does not raise the denial. He asks lovest thou me, and after each answer gives a commission — feed my lambs, feed my sheep. Restoration here is accomplished by being fed and then being given work. Luke 11:37 shows the other kind of meal: Christ dines with a Pharisee, declines the ceremonial washing, and delivers six woes at the table. Both meals are pastoral; they are simply addressed to different conditions.
roots_summary: Greek aristao (G709), to take the morning or chief meal; ariston (G712), dinner; Hebrew idiom in Genesis 43:16, they shall eat with me at noon.
roots_lines: Greek aristao (G709) — to dine; John 21:12, 15, Luke 11:37.
Greek ariston (G712) — dinner, the chief meal; Luke 11:38, 14:12.
Greek anthrakia (G439) — a fire of coals; John 18:18 and 21:9, the only two occurrences.
usage: “Come and dine” — restoration beginning with breakfast.
“He marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner” — and six woes followed.
“These men shall dine with me at noon” — Joseph's brothers, not yet knowing him.

etymology: From Latin dispergere, to scatter abroad. Scripture uses dispersal as judgment, as mission, and once as the method of generosity.
biblical_def: To disperse is to scatter. Jacob foretells that Simeon and Levi shall be scattered in Israel (Gen 49:7). Ezekiel says God dispersed the people among the countries and will gather them again (Eze 20:23; 36:19). Proverbs uses it of generosity: “There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth” (Pro 11:24), and Paul quotes the psalm, “He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever” (2Co 9:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disperse as to scatter; to drive asunder; to cause to separate into different parts; to diffuse, to spread; and to dissipate.
webster_full: DISPERSE, v.t. To scatter; to drive asunder; to cause to separate into different parts; as, the Jews are dispersed among all nations.
2. To diffuse; to spread.
3. To dissipate; as, the fog or the cloud is dispersed.
scriptures: (As it is written, He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever.
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
And I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries: according to their way and according to their doings I judged them.
Gen 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
corruption_summary: Accumulation is treated as the way to hold wealth, and Scripture's word for the righteous man's handling of it is dispersal.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 9:9 quotes Psalm 112 and the verb is startling for a passage about money: he hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever. Dispersal is normally what happens to something being lost. Here it is the method by which something permanent is established — the goods scatter and the righteousness remains. Paul uses it to encourage a collection, and the logic is agricultural: he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.

Ezekiel 36:19 shows the darker use and its reversal in the same chapter: I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries. Then, twenty verses later, I will take you from among the heathen, and gather you out of all countries, and will bring you into your own land. Dispersal and gathering are both God's acts, and the chapter's centre is the promise of a new heart and a new spirit.
roots_summary: Hebrew pazar (H6340), to scatter, disperse; puts (H6327), to scatter; Greek skorpizo (G4650), to scatter.
roots_lines: Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter, disperse; Psalm 112:9, Proverbs 11:24.
Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter abroad; Ezekiel 36:19, Genesis 11:8.
Greek skorpizo (G4650) — to scatter; 2 Corinthians 9:9, John 10:12.
usage: “He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor” — scattering that establishes.
“There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth” — the economics of the openhanded.
“I scattered them… I will gather you” — both acts God's.

etymology: Dis- with honour. Dishonour is honour withheld or reversed, and Paul makes it a category in both the potter's house and the resurrection.
biblical_def: Dishonour is disgrace. Christ says, “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house” (Mat 13:57), and tells His accusers, “I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me” (Joh 8:49). Paul asks the Jews who boast in the law, “through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?” (Rom 2:23). He describes vessels “one to honour, and another unto dishonour” (Rom 9:21), and says the body “is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory” (1Co 15:43).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dishonor as reproach; disgrace; ignominy; shame; whatever constitutes a stain or blemish in the reputation.
webster_full: DISHONOR, n. Reproach; disgrace; ignominy; shame; whatever constitutes a stain or blemish in the reputation.
DISHONOR, v.t. To disgrace; to bring reproach or shame on; to stain the character of; to lessen reputation.
2. To treat with indignity.
scriptures: Joh 8:49
Jesus answered, I have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me.
Rom 2:23
Thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?
It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:
And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
corruption_summary: Believers guard their own honour and are careless with God's, and Paul asks a religious audience whether their law-breaking dishonours the God they boast in.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 2:23-24 aims at the religiously respectable: thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God? For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you. The dishonour is not done by the world's opposition but by the inconsistency of God's own people, and the damage lands on His reputation among outsiders. That is a heavier charge than any the passage makes against pagans.

1 Corinthians 15:43 uses the word without any moral sting: it is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory. Paul is describing burial. A corpse is dishonourable in the plain sense — it must be covered and put away — and the resurrection is stated as the reversal of exactly that condition. The verse dignifies grief by naming the indignity honestly before promising its undoing.

usage: “I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me” — the charge answered plainly.
“Through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?” — aimed at the religious.
